events.title: Back in five
events.text: An old claim beacon on a rock the size of a bed, ticking over on a cell somebody forgot to take. The rock has been worked out to the last vein: a tidy hole, a lamp left burning, a tin cup in a bracket. There is a file in the beacon's memory, and nobody left to say whose it is.

outcomes.text: The beacon holds one file, left by the last person to work the rock. You read it by the lamp they left on.
The beacon's last file is a page of somebody's diary, filed under RULES. The tin cup is still in its bracket.
Somebody left a galley sheet in the beacon's memory, for reasons that are probably soup. The cup, you notice, has been used.
The last file is a collection receipt in a cramped hand, filed under MA. Everybody out here has one of those.
You leave the beacon ticking in its hole. The lamp is still lit when you lose it on the scope. Somebody may come back for it. Somebody may.

events.title: Relay, unattended
events.text: A Concord relay buoy, powered and polished, forwarding nothing to nobody. Its status board is green. It has been green for forty years, and it still sends a heartbeat every nine seconds to a station that is not there. In its outbox, one file is waiting to send.

outcomes.text: The outbox opens without a password, as if it had been waiting for someone to ask. You read the file.
The relay's outbox holds a patrol log marked NO ACTION. It was never sent, which is the most Concord thing about it.
A requisition form, filled in, never sent. The relay has been trying for forty years. You read it so it can stop.
A diplomatic annex in the outbox: eleven hours of argument reduced to four lines. You read it for the four lines.
You leave the relay to its heartbeat. Nine seconds later it sends another, and the quiet where the answer should be is very well kept.

events.title: A buoy that sings because someone must
events.text: A Lumen buoy turns in the dark, singing one long note and then stopping to wait, politely, for an answer. It sounds like a question. The pause is the right length for a reply. Nobody is on the other end to give it one, and the buoy has, you suspect, stopped expecting anybody to.

outcomes.text: You hum something back, badly. The buoy considers it, and releases a short text it has been keeping for whoever answered.
The pause lengthens. A panel in the casing slides open and a small slate falls out, written in a neat hand.
The buoy sings the same note again, slower, and a file you did not ask for opens on the console.
The buoy hums a flat, offended note when you switch the engines on, and then, grudgingly, a file.
The note falls. A line of text appears on the console in the buoy's careful hand, with the air of a complaint finally forwarded.
You let the pause run out. The buoy sings its note again, a little lower, to nobody, and carries on waiting.

events.title: To whoever
events.text: A sealed cargo tube, welded to a rock with a lot of caution and not much skill, marked TO WHOEVER. Inside, a data slug, a tin of the blue ration, and a handwritten label: PLEASE READ. IT'S NOT THE BAD KIND.

outcomes.text: You break the weld, which is more than the weld wanted, and read the slug. Whoever wrote it did not think anyone would.
The slug is a page of somebody's life, filed under DUES. You eat the ration, to be fair.
The slug is a letter to somebody who will never get it. You eat the ration, because the label asked you to.
The slug is a warning, and also, you realise, a joke. You eat the ration anyway.
The slug is a day's log kept by somebody who had decided to find it funny. You eat the ration, and take the tone.
You leave the tube on its rock, welded, for the next one. It said PLEASE READ. Somebody will.
